analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax subsidies for large ethanol fuel producers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and expired when the 104th Congress ended; the ethanol tax credit stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal tax law gave a credit for every gallon of ethanol blended into motor fuel, on top of a reduced excise tax rate for alcohol fuels. This bill would have ended the credit for large producers after 1997, denied the credit for alcohol used to make ethers, and taxed fuel alcohol like any other motor fuel. It would also have imposed a one-time tax of 18.4 cents per gallon on large stockpiles of fuel alcohol held when the change took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would stop paying for a per-gallon credit that goes to large ethanol producers and fuel blenders. The change was set for January 1, 1998, with small-producer credits left intact.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the per-gallon income tax credit for large producers of ethanol used as fuel after 1997, ending a taxpayer-funded subsidy.
Denies the credit for alcohol used to produce ethers and repeals the reduced excise tax rates on alcohol fuels, so fuel alcohol is taxed the same as gasoline and diesel.
Repeals the reduced rate for ethanol fuel produced from natural gas, closing a route by which fossil-derived fuel qualified for the alcohol-fuel break.
Retains the separate credit for small ethanol producers, so the cut targets the largest producers rather than the smallest operations.

analysis.who_pays: Large ethanol producers and fuel blenders, who would lose the per-gallon credit and the reduced excise rate, and anyone holding more than 2,000 gallons of fuel alcohol on the effective date, who would owe a one-time 18.4-cents-per-gallon floor stock tax. Drivers using ethanol-based alternative fuels would pay the full motor fuel tax going forward.

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes fuel alcohol like gasoline and imposes a one-time 18.4-cents-per-gallon tax on stockpiles over 2,000 gallons, raising costs for users of ethanol-based alternative fuels.
The ethanol credit was defended as support for an alternative fuel and for farm-based energy; ending it could make ethanol less price-competitive with gasoline and reduce demand for corn-based fuel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main effect is saving taxpayer money by ending a subsidy aimed at large producers, while keeping the small-producer credit. The costs are real but narrow: a one-time tax on fuel stockpiles and full taxation of ethanol fuel going forward. On balance it is a straightforward subsidy cut, though critics would note it also withdraws support from alternative fuels generally.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English introduced the bill on November 16, 1995, with three cosponsors: Rep. Montgomery, Rep. Miller of Florida, and Rep. Zimmer.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large ethanol producers and fuel blenders, who kept the per-gallon tax credit and reduced excise rates that the bill would have ended; the credit continued to be paid out of federal tax collections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large ethanol producers kept their credit

sides.party_line_note: Support was a small bipartisan group of five House members (4 Republicans and 1 Democrat), and no votes were ever taken, so no party-line pattern exists in the record.

industries.industry: Large ethanol producers and fuel blenders
industries.note: The bill would end their per-gallon tax credit and reduced excise rate after 1997, subsidies that ordinary taxpayers effectively fund. Their gain from the status quo is the public's cost.
The bill preserves the separate small-producer credit while eliminating the large-producer credit, leaving the smallest operations' subsidy untouched.

industries.industry: Users of ethanol and methanol alternative fuels
industries.note: Fuel alcohol would pay the full motor fuel excise tax, plus a one-time 18.4-cents-per-gallon tax on stockpiles over 2,000 gallons, raising costs for alternative-fuel drivers and boat owners.
